titleStmt.title: Neuronal connectivity and interactions between the auditory and limbic systems. Effects of noise and tinnitus
titleStmt.author: Kraus
Canlon

publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: Neuronal connectivity and interactions between the auditory and limbic systems. Effects of noise and tinnitus

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: mechanism
span.quote: Acoustic experience such as sound, noise, or absence of sound induces structural or functional changes in the central auditory system but can also affect limbic regions such as the amygdala and hippocampus.

span.label: auditory-limbic interaction under noise and tinnitus
span.quote: The acoustic environment also affects non-auditory brain regions such as the limbic system.

span.label: review
span.quote: In this review we will present current knowledge on auditoryelimbic interactions, with emphasis on noise-the aversive acoustic stimuli from an external source, as well as the internally generated phantom sound of tinnitus.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Noise activates the amygdala, which drives the HPA axis to release glucocorticoids, which then act on receptors throughout the body including the inner ear
span.quote: Exposure to noise can trigger the release of glucocorticoids by activation of the HPA-axis via the amygdala (Fig. 4).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Noise drives neural hyperactivity in the hippocampus, and this hyperactivity (rather than circulating stress hormone) suppresses neurogenesis over the long term
span.quote: Therefore it is conceivable that neural hyperactivity in hippocampus during noise exposure may play a role for altering neurogenesis long-term.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Fear conditioning is implemented by long-term potentiation of lateral amygdala pyramidal neurons via NMDA receptors and voltage-gated calcium channels
span.quote: The mechanism for fear conditioning is proposed to be long-term potentiation on pyramidal neurons in lateral amygdala, and formation of long-term memory by involvement of NMDA receptors together with voltage gated calcium channels (Blair et al., 2001).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Acute stress protects the ear because released glucocorticoids activate glucocorticoid receptors in inner-ear tissue before the traumatic sound arrives
span.quote: It is believed that the protection against noise trauma is through the activation of glucocorticoid receptors in the inner ear (Canlon et al., 2007; Meltser and Canlon, 2011).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: An amygdala-to-auditory feedback loop (via nucleus accumbens and thalamic reticular nucleus) gates the tinnitus signal out before it reaches cortex and awareness
span.quote: A feedback pathway from the amygdala to the auditory system may suppress the tinnitus signal at a subcortical level before it reaches auditory cortex and consciousness (Rauschecker et al., 2010).

span.label: Direct evidence that the limbic system is essential to tinnitus generation or stabilisation is not established.
span.quote: However, direct evidence for this is not well established (Adjamian et al., 2009).

span.label: Responses to noise vary widely between individuals and depend strongly on the type of noise.
span.note: what this limits: any general statement about noise effects: RESPONSES TO NOISE MAY HUGELY VARY AMONG INDIVIDUALS AND HEAVILY DEPEND ON THE TYPE OF NOISE
span.quote: While responses to noise may hugely vary among individuals (Belojevic et al., 2003) and heavily depend on the type of noise (Irwin et al., 2010), there is general evidence on negative effects of acute as well as chronic noise on brain and health.

span.label: Whether amygdalar activity facilitates or inhibits auditory cortex depends on unresolved further factors.
span.note: what this limits: the direction of the amygdala's effect on auditory cortex: HOW AMYGDALA-ACTIVITY AFFECTS AUDITORY CORTEX ACTIVITY OR PLASTICITY DEPENDS ON FURTHER CIRCUMSTANCES, SUCH AS WHICH AMYGDALAR NEURONS ARE ACTIVATED, OR WHICH OTHER BRAIN REGIONS ARE CO-ACTIVATED
span.quote: Thus, how amygdala-activity affects auditory cortex activity or plasticity depends on further circumstances, such as which amygdalar neurons are activated, or which other brain regions are co-activated.

span.label: The crucial feature for the response is stated to be the stimulus pattern, not the emotion it produces.
span.note: what this limits: any emotional interpretation of amygdalar activation reported here: the authors state the findings suggest the stimulus pattern itself, and not the resulting emotion, is the crucial feature
span.quote: These findings suggest that the stimulus pattern itself and not the resulting emotion is the crucial feature for amygdalar activation

span.label: The direction of the amygdala's effect on auditory cortex is unresolved, and the paper names what it turns on.
span.note: what this limits: any claim that amygdalar activity facilitates or inhibits auditory cortex: the effect is said to depend on further circumstances, namely which amygdalar neurons are activated and which other brain regions are co-activated
span.quote: Thus, how amygdala-activity affects auditory cortex activity or plasticity depends on further circumstances, such as which amygdalar neurons are activated, or which other brain regions are co-activated

span.label: The hippocampal claim is split between storage and retrieval by a single-patient observation.
span.note: what this limits: any claim that memory depends on the hippocampus: the cited case shows memory storage but not memory retrieval to be dependent on hippocampus, since the patient could still remember events from before surgery
span.quote: In contrast, he remained capable of remembering events from before surgery, showing that memory storage but not memory retrieval is dependent on hippocampus

span.label: stimulus pattern
span.quote: These findings suggest that the stimulus pattern itself and not the resulting emotion is the crucial feature for amygdalar activation

span.label: amygdalar activation
span.quote: These findings suggest that the stimulus pattern itself and not the resulting emotion is the crucial feature for amygdalar activation

span.label: amygdala-activity
span.quote: Thus, how amygdala-activity affects auditory cortex activity or plasticity depends on further circumstances, such as which amygdalar neurons are activated, or which other brain regions are co-activated

span.label: auditory cortex
span.quote: Thus, how amygdala-activity affects auditory cortex activity or plasticity depends on further circumstances, such as which amygdalar neurons are activated, or which other brain regions are co-activated

span.label: memory storage
span.quote: In contrast, he remained capable of remembering events from before surgery, showing that memory storage but not memory retrieval is dependent on hippocampus

span.label: amygdalar activation - DRIVEN BY THE STIMULUS PATTERN, NOT THE EMOTION: the review reports that responses to emotionally meaningful sounds occur independently of how emotionally involved the subject is, and concludes the pattern itself is the crucial feature, so an 'emotional response' here names a reaction to an acoustic form
span.quote: These findings suggest that the stimulus pattern itself and not the resulting emotion is the crucial feature for amygdalar activation

span.label: the amygdala's effect on auditory cortex - SIGNED ONLY ONCE THE CIRCUMSTANCES ARE FIXED: whether it facilitates or inhibits depends on which amygdalar neurons fire and which other regions are co-active, so the relation has no direction stated in the abstract and two possible directions in the body
span.quote: Thus, how amygdala-activity affects auditory cortex activity or plasticity depends on further circumstances, such as which amygdalar neurons are activated, or which other brain regions are co-activated

span.label: hippocampal dependence - STORAGE BUT NOT RETRIEVAL: the cited patient could still remember events from before surgery, which splits 'memory depends on the hippocampus' into a claim that holds for one half of the process and fails for the other
span.quote: In contrast, he remained capable of remembering events from before surgery, showing that memory storage but not memory retrieval is dependent on hippocampus

span.label: contradicts → He et al. (2004)
span.note: differs in: THE SIGN OF THE EFFECT. The review has just reported amygdalar activity FACILITATING auditory cortex, and then: 'ON THE CONTRARY, rat studies have demonstrated that stimulation of lateral amygdala CAN INHIBIT THE RESPONSE OF PRIMARY AUDITORY CORTEX TO SOUND via GABA receptors.' Two directions for one connection, and the review does not resolve them - the record already carries that as a sense, marked as signed only once the circumstances are fixed
span.quote: On the contrary, rat studies have demonstrated that stimulation of lateral amygdala can inhibit the response of primary auditory cortex to sound via GABA receptors (He et al., 2004).

span.label: builds-on → Sander et al. (2003)
span.note: differs in: WHAT THE AMYGDALA IS RESPONDING TO. 'These findings suggest that THE STIMULUS PATTERN ITSELF AND NOT THE RESULTING EMOTION is the crucial feature for amygdalar activation.' The structure that carries the emotional interpretation of the literature turns out to be driven by an acoustic property, so results reported as emotional responses may be pattern responses under an emotional description
span.quote: These findings suggest that the stimulus pattern itself and not the resulting emotion is the crucial feature for amygdalar activation (Sander et al., 2003).

span.label: builds-on → Mizuno and Giese (2005)
span.note: differs in: WHICH HALF OF MEMORY THE STRUCTURE IS NEEDED FOR, SPLIT BY ONE PATIENT'S PRESERVED ABILITY: 'IN CONTRAST, HE REMAINED CAPABLE OF REMEMBERING EVENTS FROM BEFORE SURGERY, showing that MEMORY STORAGE BUT NOT MEMORY RETRIEVAL IS DEPENDENT ON HIPPOCAMPUS.' A single dissociation does the work of dividing one word into two functions, which is a large claim to rest on what a patient could still do
span.quote: In contrast, he remained capable of remembering events from before surgery, showing that memory storage but not memory retrieval is dependent on hippocampus (Mizuno and Giese, 2005).

span.label: amygdala-activity —causes→ auditory cortex
span.note: depends on: which amygdalar neurons are activated, and which other brain regions are co-activated · strength of the relation: 0.6 — the record marks this weak
span.quote: Thus, how amygdala-activity affects auditory cortex activity or plasticity depends on further circumstances, such as which amygdalar neurons are activated, or which other brain regions are co-activated

span.label: The review concludes that the limbic system contributes to both the generation and the suppression of tinnitus, making it a target for treatment.
span.quote: In turn, the limbic system may play a role in the generation as well as the suppression of tinnitus indicating that the limbic system may be essential for tinnitus treatment.

span.label: Amygdalar activation by emotionally meaningful sound is driven by the acoustic stimulus pattern itself rather than by the emotion the listener feels.
span.quote: These findings suggest that the stimulus pattern itself and not the resulting emotion is the crucial feature for amygdalar activation (Sander et al., 2003).

span.label: Although chronic stress correlates with hearing problems, acute stress is protective, improving hearing sensitivity and reducing noise-induced hearing loss.
span.quote: In summary, while there are positive correlations between stress and hearing problems, a large body of studies provides evidence that acute stress can enhance hearing or mediate protection against noise-induced hearing loss.

span.label: The effect of stress hormones on hippocampal LTP follows an inverted-U dose relationship, facilitating potentiation at low levels and impairing it at high levels.
span.quote: Stress hormone effects on hippocampal plasticity were originally described as an “inverted U shaped curve”: At low stress hormone levels, a hormone increase facilitates LTP while at high stress hormone levels a further increase impairs LTP (Lynch, 2004; Maggio and Segal, 2010).

span.label: Because corticosterone returns to baseline soon after noise while neurogenesis stays suppressed for weeks, sustained stress-hormone elevation cannot be the cause of the long-term neurogenesis deficit.
span.quote: Thus the long-term neurogenesis reduction after noise cannot be mediated by sustained corticosterone elevation (Hayes et al., 2011).

span.label: Hippocampal phase-locking to auditory input is novelty-dependent, appearing for new stimuli and declining with repetition, which suggests a role in novelty detection.
span.quote: Furthermore, studies in guinea pig showed that phaselocking occurs when a stimulus is novel, but declines with repetition suggesting that phase-locking may play a role in the identification of novel stimuli (Liberman et al., 2009).

span.label: Stress has opposite effects on the two memory operations: it strengthens encoding of emotionally arousing events while suppressing retrieval and cognition.
span.quote: In summary, stress is capable of enhancing memory of emotionally arousing situations while it inhibits memory retrieval or cognition.

span.label: acoustic startle response
span.quote: The acoustic startle response is a rapid body twitch (startle) in response to a sudden loud sound and it is known that the amygdala can regulate the amplitude of the acoustic startle response.

span.label: pre-pulse inhibition
span.quote: Additionally, the basolateral amygdala can reduce the startle amplitude through “pre-pulse inhibition”, a suppression of the startle response by a weaker stimulus immediately before the startle-eliciting stimulus.

span.label: hippocampal inhibition or gating
span.quote: When identical auditory stimuli are repeated the response of the hippocampus decreases, a mechanism called hippocampal inhibition or gating.

span.label: neurogenesis
span.quote: Neurogenesis, the generation of new neurons, occurs in the subgranular zone of the DG and these new-born granule cells are then integrated into the existing circuits (Kempermann, 2002; Ge et al., 2008).

span.label: Pavlovian fear conditioning
span.quote: Of particular importance is the Pavlovian fear conditioning (Maren, 2003, 2005; Sah et al., 2003; Rodrigues et al., 2004; Rosen, 2004) where a meaningless or neutral stimulus (conditioned stimulus) is coupled with the response network by an unpleasant stimulus (unconditioned stimulus) so that eventually the conditioned stimulus alone triggers the response.

span.label: place cells
span.quote: Hippocampal pyramidal cells, also known as “place cells”, fire dependently on the location of in threedimensional space.

span.label: 126 dB, 12 kHz narrowband, 2 h — the single acute noise exposure that produced a hippocampal neurogenesis reduction still visible ten weeks later
span.quote: Rats exposed to a high-intensity noise (126 dB, 12 kHz narrowband, 2 h) also showed a long-lasting reduction of hippocampal neurogenesis as seen 10 weeks after exposure (Kraus et al., 2010).

span.label: 30 days / 40 days — recovery time of hippocampal monoamine levels and memory after 80 dB versus 100 dB chronic noise, showing recovery scales with exposure intensity
span.quote: The rate of recovery was dependent on the intensity of noise where rats exposed to 80 dB needed 30 days to recover while rats exposed to 100 dB needed 40 days.

span.label: 2.1 kHz — the fundamental frequency of rat pain calls to which lateral amygdala neurons phase-lock
span.quote: Species-specific pain calls (tail-pain chatter) causes neuronal responses in the lateral amygdala that are phase-locked with the fundamental frequency (2.1 kHz) of the calls in anesthetized rats (Du et al., 2009).

span.label: 80 dB, 2 h, 6 weeks — the moderate noise dose sufficient to impair learning and memory and cause oxidative damage
span.quote: Moreover, even moderately intense noise (80 dB, 2 h, 6 weeks) impaired learning and memory as assessed using the water maze and avoidance tasks.

span.label: 122 dB — the noise level after which sympathectomy reduced permanent threshold shift in guinea pigs
span.quote: Sympathectomy was found to reduce a permanent threshold shift after 122 dB noise exposure in guinea pigs (Hildesheimer et al., 2002).

p.note: The full text of this article is not redistributable, so it is not included here. Every tag above carries the exact sentence it was made from, quoted under fair quotation. The article itself is at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.heares.2012.02.009.
